topic.title: Linux Administration
topic.description: Processes, services, logs, disks, files and permissions on Linux servers

commands.name: ps
commands.description: Prints a one-time snapshot of processes. BSD-style options (aux) and standard options (-ef, -o) can select and format columns.

flags.description: BSD style: processes of all users that have a terminal.
BSD style: user-oriented format with %CPU, %MEM, VSZ and RSS.
BSD style: include processes without a terminal (daemons).
Sort by a column; prefix with - for descending.

examples.title: All processes with resource usage
examples.scenario: The server is slow. List every process with user, CPU and memory usage.
examples.explanation: a: all users, u: user-oriented columns, x: include daemons without a terminal.
examples.output:
USER       PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY  STAT START TIME COMMAND
root         1  0.0  0.1 168000 12800 ?    Ss   09:01 0:02 /sbin/init
www-data  1421  2.3  0.5  88320 43120 ?    S    09:02 0:13 nginx: worker

output_notes.meaning: Resident memory in KiB actually held in RAM.
output_notes.anomaly: Steady growth over hours: likely leak.

output_notes.meaning: Process state: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible I/O wait, Z zombie.

examples.title: Top memory consumers
examples.scenario: Find which processes use the most memory, largest first.
examples.explanation: --sort=-%mem orders by memory descending; head keeps the first 10 lines.

examples.title: Custom columns for one PID
examples.scenario: Show PID, parent PID, state, CPU, memory and command line for process 3100.
examples.explanation: -o picks the columns, -p selects the process.

use_cases.title: Load spike
use_cases.situation: Identify the process responsible for a sudden CPU or memory spike.

use_cases.title: Zombie hunting
use_cases.situation: Find defunct processes and their parent with ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm.

pitfalls: %CPU is averaged over the process lifetime, not the current instant; use top for live usage.

commands.name: systemctl
commands.summary: Control systemd services and inspect their state
commands.description: Starts, stops, restarts and inspects systemd units and controls whether they start at boot.

flags.description: State, main PID, recent log lines of a unit.
Ask the service to reload its configuration without stopping.
Start the unit at boot; --now also starts it immediately.
Print active/inactive; exit code 0 when active.
Reload unit files after editing them.

examples.title: Service status
examples.scenario: Check whether nginx is running and see its latest log lines.
examples.output:
● nginx.service - A high performance web server
     Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Thu 2026-11-19 09:02:11 UTC; 1 day ago
   Main PID: 1419 (nginx)

output_notes.anomaly: disabled: will not come back after reboot.

examples.title: Restart a service
examples.scenario: Apply a new configuration by restarting the api service.

examples.title: Enable and start
examples.scenario: Make nginx start at boot and start it right now.

examples.title: Failed units
examples.scenario: After a reboot, list every unit that failed to start.

use_cases.title: Service down after deploy
use_cases.situation: Confirm the unit state and read the last log lines in one view.

use_cases.title: Post-reboot check
use_cases.situation: Ensure no unit failed after maintenance.

pitfalls: After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload before restarting, or the old definition is used.

commands.name: journalctl
commands.description: Reads logs collected by systemd-journald, filtered by unit, time, priority or boot.

flags.description: Start time, e.g. "1 hour ago" or "2026-11-20 10:00".
Current boot only; -b -1 for the previous boot.
Print without the pager (useful in scripts).

examples.title: Follow a unit's logs
examples.scenario: Watch the api service logs live while reproducing an error.

examples.title: Logs from the last hour
examples.scenario: Read nginx logs from the last hour only.

examples.title: Errors in this boot
examples.scenario: List every error-level message since the last boot.

examples.title: Previous boot tail
examples.scenario: The server rebooted unexpectedly. Show the last 50 lines of the previous boot.

use_cases.title: Unexpected reboot
use_cases.situation: Inspect the end of the previous boot for OOM or kernel panics.

use_cases.title: Crash loop
use_cases.situation: Follow a unit while systemd restarts it to capture the failure.

pitfalls: Without persistent storage (/var/log/journal), previous boots are not kept.

commands.name: df
commands.description: Reports used and available space and inodes for mounted filesystems.

examples.title: Disk usage per mount
examples.scenario: Writes are failing. Check free space on every mounted filesystem.
examples.output:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/vda1        50G   48G  2.0G  97% /
/dev/vdb1       200G   61G  139G  31% /data

output_notes.anomaly: > 90%: writes and logs will soon fail.

examples.title: Inode exhaustion
examples.scenario: Disk shows free space but files cannot be created. Check inode usage.
examples.explanation: Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while blocks are still free.

examples.title: Filesystem types
examples.scenario: List mounts with their filesystem type in human-readable sizes.

use_cases.title: No space left on device
use_cases.situation: Confirm which mount is full before cleaning up.

pitfalls: Deleted files still held open by a process keep using space; check with lsof +L1.

commands.name: du
commands.summary: Disk usage of files and directories
commands.description: Estimates space used by files and directories, recursively.

examples.title: Largest directories one level deep
examples.scenario: /var is full. Show the size of each directory directly under it.
examples.explanation: -d 1 limits depth; sort -h orders human-readable sizes.

examples.title: Total size of a directory
examples.scenario: How much space does /var/log use in total?

examples.title: Stay on the root filesystem
examples.scenario: Find what fills / without descending into other mounts.

use_cases.title: Find what filled the disk
use_cases.situation: Drill down directory by directory until the culprit appears.

pitfalls: du and df can disagree when deleted files are still open.

commands.name: free
commands.description: Shows total, used and available memory and swap.

examples.title: Memory overview
examples.scenario: Check how much memory is really available for new processes.
examples.output:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           7.7Gi       5.9Gi       210Mi        12Mi       1.6Gi       1.5Gi
Swap:          2.0Gi       1.1Gi       0.9Gi

output_notes.meaning: Memory usable by new processes without swapping (includes reclaimable cache).

output_notes.anomaly: Growing swap with low available memory: thrashing.

examples.title: Sample every 5 seconds
examples.scenario: Watch memory every 5 seconds during a load test.

use_cases.title: OOM investigation
use_cases.situation: Confirm memory pressure before looking for the consumer with ps.

pitfalls: Low 'free' is normal: Linux uses spare RAM as cache. Read 'available'.

commands.name: lsof
commands.summary: List open files, sockets and their processes
commands.description: Lists files opened by processes; in Linux, sockets and pipes are files too.

examples.title: Who uses a port
examples.scenario: nginx cannot bind port 80. Find which process already uses it.

examples.title: Deleted but open files
examples.scenario: df shows a full disk but du does not. Find deleted files still held open.

examples.title: Files of a process
examples.scenario: Count how many files process 3100 has open.

use_cases.title: Address already in use
use_cases.situation: Identify the process holding a port before restarting a service.

use_cases.title: Too many open files
use_cases.situation: Measure open descriptors against the process limit.

commands.name: find
commands.summary: Search the filesystem by name, size, age or type
commands.description: Walks directory trees and selects files matching tests; can run actions on them.

flags.description: Modified more/less than N days ago.

examples.title: Files larger than 1 GB
examples.scenario: Find files larger than 1 GB under /var.

examples.title: Old compressed logs
examples.scenario: List compressed logs older than 30 days in /var/log/app.

examples.title: Delete old temp files
examples.scenario: Delete files in /tmp/app older than 7 days.

use_cases.title: Disk cleanup
use_cases.situation: Locate oversized or stale files before freeing space.

pitfalls: Run the expression without -delete first to review what would be removed.

examples.title: Errors with context
examples.scenario: Show each 'timeout' (any case) in app.log with 3 lines of context.

examples.title: Search a config tree
examples.scenario: Find where listen ports are configured under /etc/nginx, with line numbers.

use_cases.situation: Narrow a large log to the lines around a failure.

commands.name: tail
commands.summary: Show the end of a file, optionally following it
commands.description: Prints the last lines of files and can follow growth in real time.

flags.description: Follow and reopen when the file is rotated.

examples.title: Follow a log through rotation
examples.scenario: Watch /var/log/nginx/error.log live, surviving log rotation.

examples.title: Last 200 lines
examples.scenario: Show the last 200 lines of /var/log/app.log.

use_cases.title: Live debugging
use_cases.situation: Watch errors while reproducing a request.

commands.name: chmod
commands.description: Sets read/write/execute permissions with octal (640) or symbolic (u+x) modes.

flags.description: Symbolic: add execute for the owner.
Octal: owner rw, group r, others none.

examples.title: Make a script executable
examples.scenario: Allow the owner to execute deploy.sh.

examples.title: Protect a private key
examples.scenario: SSH refuses id_ed25519 because it is too open. Restrict it to the owner.

examples.title: Readable by the service group
examples.scenario: Let the owner write and the group read /etc/app/config.yml, others nothing.

use_cases.title: Permission denied
use_cases.situation: Fix modes after copying files with the wrong umask.

pitfalls: Avoid chmod -R 777: it exposes files to every user and hides the real ownership problem.

commands.name: chown
commands.description: Changes the owning user and/or group of files.

examples.title: Give the web root to www-data
examples.scenario: Make www-data the owner and group of /var/www/app, recursively.

examples.title: Change only the group
examples.scenario: Set the group of /srv/backup to 'backup' without changing the owner.

use_cases.title: Upload fails with 403
use_cases.situation: The service user cannot write into a directory owned by root.

commands.name: kill
commands.description: Sends a signal (TERM by default) to processes; also used to pause and resume them.

flags.description: Immediate kill that cannot be caught (9).
Hang-up; many daemons reload configuration on it.

examples.title: Graceful stop
examples.scenario: Ask process 3100 to terminate gracefully.

examples.title: Force kill
examples.scenario: Process 3100 ignored TERM for a minute. Kill it immediately.

examples.title: Reload configuration
examples.scenario: Make the nginx master process (PID 1419) reload its configuration.

use_cases.title: Hung worker
use_cases.situation: Stop a stuck worker after TERM fails.

pitfalls: KILL skips cleanup (temp files, locks, flushes). Try TERM first.

flags.description: Change to a directory before acting.

examples.title: Back up a directory

examples.title: Inspect before extracting
examples.scenario: List the contents of app.tar.gz without extracting.

commands.name: uptime
commands.description: Shows how long the system has run and the 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages.

examples.title: Load averages
examples.scenario: Get a quick sense of system load and how long it has been up.

output_notes.meaning: Average runnable plus uninterruptible tasks over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
output_notes.anomaly: 1-minute value well above the vCPU count and rising.

use_cases.title: First look
use_cases.situation: Is the box overloaded, and did it reboot recently?

pitfalls: Processes in D state (I/O wait) raise load without using CPU.
